title: The Most Expensive Assumption We Ever Made
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that the 'digital native' myth—the assumption that children born into technology naturally understand it—was the most expensive educational assumption of the past generation, and that we are about to repeat it with AI. Research by Kirschner and De Bruyckere debunked the notion that growing up with devices creates technological comprehension; what students develop is comfort, not understanding, and the gap between these looks identical from across the room. OECD data showed that fewer than one in ten fifteen-year-olds could reliably distinguish fact from opinion online despite being fully device-fluent, and the resulting harm—documented in the 2023 Surgeon General's advisory on social media and youth mental health—became population-scale. Marcinek sees the same pattern replaying with AI: seven in ten teens have used generative AI, most without parental knowledge and none with adult instruction, repeating the social media dynamic of mass adoption with zero adult guidance. His prescription is twofold: don't assume fluency, teach it deliberately as curriculum, and do so now rather than after the harm compounds. UNESCO, the EU, and ISTE have already developed AI competency frameworks; the serious institutions have landed on explicit instruction as the answer.
points: The 'digital native' myth assumed comfort with interfaces equaled comprehension of what technology was doing to and for students—a category error that Kirschner and De Bruyckere's research demolished.

Fewer than one in ten fifteen-year-olds across OECD countries could reliably distinguish fact from opinion online, despite their visible device fluency—the same gap between access and judgment that is now opening with AI.
Seven in ten teens have used generative AI without parental knowledge and without any adult ever teaching them what the tool is or how it fails—the social media pattern is replaying in real time.
Students don't know that AI systems generate plausible text rather than verified truth, or that the machine will invent a source with a straight face; access has never equaled understanding.
Serious institutions—UNESCO, the EU, ISTE—have already developed AI competency frameworks and landed on the same answer: explicit instruction as curriculum, not assumption of fluency.
quotes: We called them digital natives. Their the digital generation, they just get technology or my kid knows how to use my phone better than I do. This is what many of us assumed 15 years ago when smart phones and social media started to encroach upon our daily lives. If kids were born knowing how to navigate technology, then we didn't have to teach it. We could hand them the device and step back.

What kids actually have is comfort — fast thumbs, no fear of the interface. What they don't have, unless someone teaches it, is comprehension of what the technology is doing to them and for them. Comfort and comprehension look identical from across the room. They are not the same thing, and the gap between them is exactly where a generation got hurt.

When the OECD tested fifteen-year-olds across dozens of countries on whether they could distinguish fact from opinion in what they read online, fewer than one in ten could do it reliably. These are the same students who can run three apps at once, who live on their phones, who look — from across the room — completely fluent. They could open everything. They could evaluate almost nothing.

This is the social media pattern replaying in real time. Mass adoption by kids. Minimal awareness by adults. Zero instruction in between. We have seen this exact movie, and we know the ending, and we are watching it again with the sequel.

Ask that same confident-looking student whether the answer is right, or where it came from, or what the tool quietly got wrong, or whether they should have used it at all — and you find the same gap we found with social media. They don't know that these systems generate plausible text rather than verified truth. They don't know the machine will invent a source with a straight face. Access is not understanding. It never was.
The second pillar is a refusal: don't assume fluency. Teach it. Deliberately, as curriculum, the way we would teach anything else that matters.
